list.listitem: Suspect rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) in patients who report movements during sleep or "acting out their dreams." A simple one-item screening question is highly accurate. C

A history of REM sleep behavior disorder may begin several years to decades before the onset of daytime symptoms of a neurodegenerative disease, primarily Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) or multiple system atrophy (MSA), so patient education and careful monitoring with serial neurological exams during follow-up is warranted. C

The RBD1Q asks a single question and has LR+ 7.2 and LR- 0.07: "Have you ever been told, or suspected yourself, that you seem to 'act out your dreams' while asleep. For example, punching, flailing your arms in the air, making running movements, etc.?" B
The most important aspect of RBD management is ensuring a safe sleeping environment and minimizing dream enactment behaviors. C
Melatonin and clonazepam are effective pharmacologic therapies. B

background.definition: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by dream enactment with abnormal, excessive motor activity during REM sleep. RBD results from loss of normal skeletal muscle atonia during REM sleep, leading to dream enactment behavior characterized by excessive motor activity. These may range from simple limb twitches to violent, complex movements that may result in injury to the patient and/or sleeping partner. RBD often presents without an identifiable cause (idiopathic RBD). RBD may also be associated with antidepressant treatment or by the use or withdrawal of drugs or alcohol. Symptomatic RBD is strongly associated with neurodegenerative diseases, often preceding other characteristic neurological manifestations by several years to decades. Autonomic dysfunction, particularly orthostatic hypotension and constipation, are early markers of progressive neurodegeneration in patients with idiopathic RBD.

list.listitem: The prevalence of RBD has been estimated between 0.38% and 0.5% in large population-based studies, but occurs in 4% to 6% of individuals over age 60.
The mean age of onset of RBD is in the 5th to 6th decade, often occurring earlier in patients taking antidepressant medications or with psychiatric disease.
RBD is most common in elderly men, except in patients with multiple system atrophy, narcolepsy, or in early-onset cases (patients taking antidepressant medications, or with psychiatric illness).
In the middle-to-older age population the prevalence of RBD did not show significant difference between men and women.
Neurodegenerative processes: especially the synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA).,,,
REM sleep behavior disorder was a presenting symptom in 28% of a series of 158 patients with MSA.
Idiopathic/cryptogenic: these patients merit long-term follow-up since idiopathic RBD often precedes development of a neurodegenerative disease by years to decades, up to 50 years.,,,
Other destructive brainstem processes or brainstem lesions: neoplasm, multiple sclerosis (MS), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP).

Antidepressant medications and depression: SSRIs and tricyclics most common, also MAOIs, and SNRIs. Cholinesterase inhibitors, beta-blockers, caffeine, and chocolate have also been known to trigger RBD episodes.

Paraneoplastic disorders: anti-voltage gated potassium channel antibody syndrome (Morvan's Syndrome, including muscle twitching, hyperhidrosis, insomnia, fluctuating cognition, and limb paresthesia with electromyographic neuromyotonia), anti-Ma2 antibody syndrome.,,,
Withdrawal of drugs including alcohol, benzodiazepines and barbiturates.
Autoimmune disease.
The dream enactment movements in RBD are due to a disruption of the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep, either due to impairment of tonic muscle atonia or due to increased phasic locomotor drive.
Animal models indicate that several different brainstem lesions may lead to motor behaviors during REM sleep.,,,

The association between RBD and the synucleinopathies suggests that these disease processes involve abnormalities of the same neuronal networks. Disturbance in dopamine and serotonergic pathways has also been implicated in both the synucleinopathies and RBD.,
Suspect rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) in patients complaining of unusual movements at night, especially if they begin after 90 minutes or more. C
The behaviors of dream enactment range from simple twitches and limb jerks to more complex behavior varying from night to night within the same individual.
Validated screening instruments such as the RBD-HK and the Mayo Sleep Questionnaire may be helpful. C

The RBD1Q asks a single question and has LR+ 7.2 and LR- 0.07: "Have you ever been told, or suspected yourself, that you seem to 'act out your dreams' while asleep. For example, punching, flailing your arms in the air, making running movements, etc.?" B

Perform a careful neurologic evaluation to rule out disorders such as Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, multiple system atrophy, seizure disorder, delirium, post-traumatic stress disorder, and sleep disorders including non-obstructive sleep apnea and narcolepsy. C

Differential.Differential_Name: OSA with arousals from REM sleep

list.listitem: The minimal diagnostic criteria according to the International Classification of Sleep Disorders include: (1) presence of REM sleep without atonia on in-lab polysomnogram, (2) sleep-related injurious or potentially injurious or disruptive behaviors by history and/or abnormal motor behaviors during REM sleep on polysomnogram, (3) absence of epileptiform activity during REM sleep unless RBD can be clearly distinguished, and (4) sleep disturbance not better explained by another disorder.
Patients and/or their bed partners may complain of violent dream-enacting behavior, often causing injury to either party. Collateral history from a sleep partner is extremely valuable.

A review of all sleep-related complaints including specific questioning about RBD symptoms is necessary to narrow the differential, and should be followed by a medical, neurologic, and psychiatric history.
Patients may remember dreaming but usually do not recall the associated movements, often reporting dream content alteration involving some sort of defense against attack, or being chased.
The behavior may spontaneously awaken the patient, potentially fragmenting sleep since a high percentage of RBD patients report excessive daytime sleepiness.
The dream enactment behaviors occur during REM sleep, therefore, episodes start around 60 to 120 minutes into sleep, and more frequently in the second half of the night.
If symptoms present acutely, consider medication-related causes if a temporal association can be established.

Patients with idiopathic RBD require a careful baseline neurologic examination with particular attention to cognitive, autonomic, and extrapyramidal signs and follow-up to screen for the development of a neurodegenerative process.,,, Mild cognitive impairment, autonomic dysfuntion, hallucinations, delusions, change in speech or volume of voice, slowing of motor activities like dressing, eating, hyposmia, constipation and postural instability are a few of the symptoms indicating concurrent neurodegenerative disorders.

Younger patients presenting with RBD should be assessed for symptoms of narcolepsy, especially when other causes such as use of antidepressants have been ruled out. All narcolepsy patients should also be asked about RBD symptoms.

The RBD1Q is a validated single question regarding dream enactment behavior with a simple yes/no answer. That question is: "Have you ever been told, or suspected yourself, that you seem to 'act out your dreams' while asleep. For example, punching, flailing your arms in the air, making running movements, etc.?" A "yes" answer is 94% sensitive and 87% specific for RBD (LR+ 7.2, LR- 0.07).

The RBD-HK is a 13-item validated measure with high internal consistency and test-retest reliability that indicates severity of parasomnia symptoms, with a cut-off score of 18 or 100 yielding positive and negative predictive values of over 80%.

The Mayo Sleep Questionnaire (MSQ) is a validated diagnostic tool for RBD screening in older patients with cognitive impairment and/or parkinsonism that is completed by an informant, typically the patient's bedpartner. The MSQ is freely available at: http://www.mayoclinic.org/pdfs/MSQ-copyrightfinal.pdf.

The gold standard for diagnosis is polysomnogram (PSG) with audiovisual recording. Utility of expanded EEG montage, and EMG of all four extremities, in the case of patients with suspected RBD, increases sensitivity and specificity of diagnosis.
A single night of PSG recording is generally sufficient, since REM sleep without atonia (RSWA) is usually evident whether or not dream-enactment behavior occurs.

An experienced interpreting polysomnongrapher is critical for the accurate identification of RSWA. RSWA may manifest as either excessive tonic or phasic transient muscle activity, with excessive phasic activity better corresponding to clinically evident behavioral events and vocalizations.

Quantitative analysis of RSWA utilizing the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) method (5 phasic muscle bursts within a 30-second epoch in either the submentalis or anterior tibialis muscles, or both) has yielded cut-off values of 34.9% to 45.1% for a diagnosis of RBD.

Investigations holding promise for predicting evolving alpha-synucleinopathy in RBD patients include dopamine transporter uptake 123I-FP-CIT SPECT DaTSCAN and transcranial sonography, neuropsychological testing, quantitative EEG, and color vision, olfactory, and autonomic testing. Clinical utility of these tests is limited.
For acute rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) in a patient taking a drug known to cause RBD, discontinue the suspected medications after consulting the prescribing physician. C

Ensure a safe sleep environment by recommending a mattress beside the bed, padded corners of furniture in the bedroom, and removal of potentially dangerous objects, such as guns, from the bedroom. The bed partner should sleep in a different room until the RBD symptoms are controlled. C
Melatonin and clonazepam are effective pharmacologic therapies with "conditional" recommendation indicating a clinical judgment is advised for use in individual patients. B

Other treatment options that have only limited evidence for improvement in symptoms include pramipexole, rotigotine, rivastigmine, donepezil, memantine, ramelteon, carbidopa-levodopa, light therapy, IVIG, positive airway pressure therapy, sodium oxybate and Yi-gan san. C
Melatonin and clonazepam are equally effective therapies for RBD.

Melatonin has been reported to have fewer side effects and contraindications than clonazepam. Side effects may include morning headache, sleepiness, and hallucinations. Melatonin may be more effective in patients with co-morbid neurodegenerative disease than clonazepam. Melatonin may affect the biology of RBD and has been shown to decrease RSWA. The median effective dose of melatonin has been reported to be 6 mg at bedtime, with a range of 3 to 12 mg having varying efficacy,
and only rarely requiring higher doses of 15 or 20 mg.

Clonazepam is an effective therapy for RBD, although it does not reestablish atonia during REM sleep. Like all benzodiazepines, clonazepam, may cause confusion, daytime sedation, increased risk for falls, mild memory impairment, dizziness and impotence in older patients and may worsen obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Therefore, clonazepam must be used with caution in all patients. The recommended dose is 0.5 to 2.0 mg taken 30 minutes before bedtime, with a reported median effective dose of 0.5 mg.
Combination of melatonin with clonazepam may also be used if clinically indicated.

Several other medications including pramipexole, rotigotine, rivastigmine, donepezil, memantine, ramelteon, carbidopa-levodopa, sodium oxybate and Yi-gan san have been used to treat RBD with variable degrees of symptom improvement. The level of evidence to support these treatments is very limited.

Treatment of underlying or secondary causes for REM sleep behavior disorder (e.g. restless legs syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea) has been shown to ameliorate symptoms of REM sleep behavior disorder.
No surgical treatment has been reported to show improvement of symptoms of RBD.

Capitalizing on characteristically rapid transitioning to alert wakefulness following REM sleep arousal, a bed alarm device that plays a prerecorded calming message may be considered to help abort RBD behavioral attacks in patients who are vulnerable to injury.

Severe injury requiring medical intervention (lacerations, fractures, subdural hematomas) occurs in 1 out of every 9 patients and frequency of dream enactment behaviors does not predict injury. Ensure a safe sleep environment by recommending a mattress beside the bed, padded corners of furniture in the bedroom, and removal of potentially dangerous objects, such as guns, knives, scissors, from the bedroom.
You may recommend that the bed partner sleep in a separate bed or room until the RBD symptoms are controlled to reduce the risk of injury.
Patients with RBD do not need to be hospitalized unless they have a serious injury caused by their nocturnal behavior.

Referral to a sleep center is appropriate for definitive diagnosis with in-lab polysomnogram and establishing a treatment plan. Neurology referral is strongly recommended for a comprehensive neurological examination of patients with idiopathic RBD, and for management of co-morbid neurodegenerative disorders in patients with symptomatic RBD.
Injuries should be treated based on the site and acuity of injury.
RBD patients with parkinsonism may benefit from trials of dopaminergic therapies, but caution is necessary in patients with concurrent orthostatic hypotension from autonomic failure.

Patients with RBD who have cognitive impairment should receive consideration for pharmacologic and behavioral therapies such as donepezil or other anticholinesterase treatments, and advice concerning driving safety or restriction when appropriate.
RBD is a prodromal feature of a neurodegenerative disorder, careful follow-up is essential. B
Over 80% of patients diagnosed with idiopathic RBD develop a neurological disorder years to decades after the onset of RBD. B

Prognosis with treatment is excellent, and treatment should usually be continued indefinitely. Occasional patients with rare or insignificant dream enactment behavior without injury history may be followed carefully without specific treatment. However, frequency and severity of dream enactment behaviors do not predict injury occurrence; therefore, RBD patients displaying infrequent behaviors may be considered for low-dose melatonin therapy in attempt to minimize risk of injury. C
Because of the likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative disease, careful neurologic follow-up is important for patients diagnosed with idiopathic RBD. C
REM sleep behavior disorder preceding onset or diagnosis of multiple system atrophy had a worse prognosis than if it appears later.
Patients diagnosed with idiopathic RBD should be counseled about the possibility of developing a neurodegenerative disorder.
Currently there are no available prevention and disease modifying treatments for these neurodegenerative disorders, multiple research studies are underway.
Disclosure of impending neurodegenerative disease should be adapted to the estimated individual conversion risk.
The majority of RBD, especially non-medication related, occurs in the elderly. Diagnosis of RBD in the elderly is similar to those in any age group.
Initiation of treatment with smaller doses is recommended as the elderly are more sensitive to the sedating adverse effects of medications including clonazepam or melatonin.
The elderly may also be more likely to present with parkinsonism, autonomic dysfunction, or cognitive impairment at diagnosis compared with those diagnosed at a younger age.

Evaluation and managment of comorbid disorders (obstructive sleep apnea, periodic limb movements, restless legs syndrome and nocturia) more commonly seen in this population will significantly improve RBD symptoms.
Little to no information available.

Treatment options may be similar to that of general population, with a greater stress on safety of the environment as medication safety has not been well established in pregnancy for benzodiazepines and melatonin.

RBD is extremely rare in children. When RBD or polysomnographic REM sleep without atonia is seen in children, symptomatic causes such as structural lesions, narcolepsy, or antidepressant medications should be suspected.,,
